statement: (a) For each $k \geq 3$, find a positive integer $n$ equal to the sum of exactly $k$ distinct positive divisors of $n$. (b) If $n$ is such a sum for some $k \geq 3$ with smallest prime divisor $p$, show $\dfrac{1}{p} + \dfrac{1}{p+1} + \cdots + \dfrac{1}{p+k-1} \geq 1$.
Convex quadrilateral $ABCD$ with $AB = AD$ and $CB = CD$. The bisector of $\angle BDC$ meets $BC$ at $L$; $AL$ meets $BD$ at $M$; $BL = BM$. Find $2\angle BAD + 3\angle BCD$.

Numbers $1, 2, \ldots, 2006$ are written around a circle. A move exchanges two adjacent numbers. After moves, each number is 13 positions to the right of its start. If $\{1,\ldots,2006\}$ is partitioned into 1003 pairs, show at least one move exchanges the two numbers of some pair.

Acute $\triangle ABC$ with $AB \neq AC$, circumcircle $\Gamma$, circumcenter $O$, orthocenter $H$. Midpoint of $BC$ is $M$; median $AM$ extended meets $\Gamma$ at $N$. Circle with diameter $AM$ meets $\Gamma$ again at $P$ (besides $A$). Show $AP$, $BC$, $OH$ are concurrent iff $AH = HN$.

Finitely many lines in the plane (no two parallel, no three concurrent) divide the plane into regions; write $1$ or $-1$ in each finite region. An operation multiplies all entries in a triangle formed by three of the lines by $-1$. Can one always reach all $1$s regardless of the initial assignment?

An infinite sequence $x_1, x_2, \ldots$ of positive integers satisfies $x_{n+2} = \gcd(x_{n+1}, x_n) + 2006$ for all $n$. Does there exist such a sequence containing exactly $10^{2006}$ distinct values?
